title: Dress rehearsal, and the sealed envelope
summary: The whole Talk, all four acts, in one take against ten minutes, with the props in your hands and nobody allowed to rescue you. Then exactly one fix. Then the motions go into an envelope nobody opens early, the judging kit gets built, and your Sprout rehearses their part twice, gently.
materials: the Expedition dossier, open at the Talk pages
the four props, one per act, out of their boxes
a camera on a tripod or propped at face height, and somewhere to watch it back
a ten minute timer, held by somebody who says nothing
the motion bank from week 9, one envelope, and a pen with real ink
blank ballots, the sand timers and the call bell
your Sprout, twice, for about ten minutes each time

steps.title: A dress rehearsal is a performance, not a practice
steps.body:
You have practised this talk in pieces for months. One act at each oasis, with a prop in your hand, in front of whoever was in the kitchen. Today is a different kind of thing and the difference is worth naming before you start.

Practice stops. You get a line wrong, you go back, you take it again. That is how a thing gets built and there is nothing wrong with it.

A dress rehearsal does not stop. Real props, real order, real clock, one take, straight through whatever happens. If you lose your place, you find it while still talking. If a prop falls on the floor, you pick it up mid-sentence. If a whole sentence comes out backwards, you keep going and you do not apologise for it, because apologising costs more time than the mistake did. That is the actual skill on offer today, and there is no way to practise it in pieces.

Then the rule that hurts. When it is over you adopt exactly one fix. Not four. One.

Here is why. A talk changed in six places is a talk you have never given. Every fix you make is a new thing to remember, and new things to remember are what fall out of a person's head when a room is looking at them. One fix, chosen because it is the biggest, gets rehearsed once more and lands. Six fixes chosen because you noticed six things arrive as six chances to freeze. Choosing which one is the whole exercise, and letting the other five go is the hard half.

This week's question sits underneath all of that: when is a thing finished? Not just this talk. Programs, drawings, plans, a shop, a card you keep revising. There is an answer that says a thing is finished when it is right, and it has an obvious problem, which is that nothing is ever quite right and people who wait for right never hand anything over. There is another answer that says a thing is finished when you decide to stop changing it and start standing behind it, and that one has its own problem, which is that you can decide too early and hand over something broken. You have been on both sides of that this year. Bring the evidence to the round.

steps.title: Ten minutes, four acts, one take
steps.body:
Set it up properly, because the setup is part of the rehearsal. Camera at about the height of a face, framed wide enough that your hands are in shot, because you are holding four things across this talk and the room is going to look at them. Props stacked in order, on a table you can reach without turning your back. One person on the timer, and their whole job is to hold it and say nothing: no signals, no mouthing the next word, no helpful laughing.

The cold open, and the listening that happens before it. The Talk is built to open with your own voice from a year ago, played to a room that has only ever met the person you are now. Two things have to happen in private this week before that goes anywhere near a guest. Somebody has to find out whether those old recordings still exist and still play, because a plan that assumes a file is a plan with a hole in it. And if they do exist, you and your Sprout listen alone, door shut, and either of you can say no. Hearing your own younger voice in front of guests is a genuinely strange thing to feel, and a no needs no explanation and gets no argument.

So rehearse the cold open both ways today. Once with the old recording, if there is one to play. Once with the standing fallback, which is you reading out loud, word for word, a page you wrote at the start of all this, from the field journal or the maker's log, in your own voice, without fixing the spelling and without apologising for any of it. The fallback is not a downgrade. A room hearing you read out your own year-old sentences gets the same jolt the recording gives, and it works whatever the storage says.

Then run the whole thing. Four acts, one per season, prop in hand for each. Ten minutes on the timer. Do not stop.

Watching it back is two jobs, not one, and doing them together means doing neither. First watch it with the sound completely off and look only at your body: hands, feet, where your eyes go, what you do with the prop when you are not using it. Then cover the screen and listen with your eyes shut: pace, the ums, where you rushed, where a sentence went on so long that even you had forgotten how it started. The two passes find different faults, which is why they are two passes.

Now choose the one fix. Say it out loud, in one sentence, so it is a decision rather than a feeling. Adopt it, then run only the act that changed, once, and stop.

One word about the clock. If it ran long, do not shave a bit off every act, because that leaves four thinner acts and no room anywhere. Cut from the act you love most. That is where the extra is, and that is why it is hard.
checklist: All four acts ran in one take with the right prop in my hand for each, and I did not stop once
Somebody held the timer and said nothing at all, and the whole take is on camera
The cold open was rehearsed both ways, with the old recording if it exists and with the read-aloud fallback
My Sprout and I listened to anything old in private first, and either of us could have said no
I watched it once with no sound and listened once with no picture, then named exactly one fix out loud and re-ran only that act

steps.title: Seal the motions, build the judging kit
steps.body:
You wrote the motion bank in week 9. Today it gets closed, and then you build the kit you will need on the day.

Read the motions through once more with one test in your hand: can a reasonable person argue either side of this without pretending? If only one side can be argued, it is not a motion, it is an announcement, and it comes out. Cut anything that fails and do not replace it, because a short bank of real motions beats a long bank with a dud in it.

Then fold them and seal the envelope. One motion gets drawn on the day and nobody knows which, including you. That is the point, and it is what makes the round worth watching: nobody in the room has had a week to build a case, so what everybody says will be what they can actually think of standing up.

The kit. Blank ballots, one per round, and more than you think. A pen that definitely works, tested today. The sand timers and the bell. And one card, written now, with the format on it, so you can announce the whole thing in twenty seconds instead of inventing it in front of people: speech lengths, who speaks first, whether a closing may carry a new argument, and what you do if somebody runs over. Decide that last one now, in the calm, and say it out loud when you announce the rules, because a rule announced in advance is a rule and a rule invented mid-round is a judge picking a side.

The ballot. Two halves, and you have used both before. While it runs you flow: what was actually said, in short lines, in the order it happened. At the end you decide, and the decision is three sentences. Name the clash, meaning the one disagreement the round really turned on. Weigh it, meaning say why that clash mattered more than the others. Then say who won and why, and stop talking.

And the rule that makes a judge worth having. You decide on what was said in the room. Not on what you happen to know is true, not on what you would have argued, and not on who you like more. If somebody drops an argument you know is wrong and nobody answers it, it stands, and your ballot says so. That is uncomfortable, and it is exactly what everybody in the room is trusting you to do.
checklist: Every motion left in the bank can honestly be argued from either side, and I cut the ones that could not
The motions are folded and the envelope is sealed, and nobody knows which one gets drawn, including me
The kit is packed: ballots, a pen I tested, the timers and the bell
The format card is written, including what happens if somebody runs over time
I can say the three sentences of a decision from memory: name the clash, weigh it, say who won and why

steps.title: Your Sprout's segment, twice, gently
steps.body:
Twice this week. Short both times. Two good goes beat five that end with somebody in tears, and you are the one deciding when to stop, which means you have to stop while it is still fun and not one minute later.

What their segment is: counting to twenty as two tens and the extras, one joining story and one taking-away story told with toys, their pattern station where they teach their own rule game to whoever is standing there, and handing their drawn page over for the Atlas.

Rehearse the shape, not the words. Where they stand. What they are holding. Who they look at. What happens when they finish, which should be something definite, like handing you the page, so they know they are done and do not stand there wondering. If you rehearse words, they will try to remember words, and forgetting a word in front of people is the exact thing that makes a young child stop dead.

Give them the job that cannot go wrong, and make it the biggest one. The pattern station is that job: they invent the rule, so whatever they make is right by definition, and the guests are the ones who might get it wrong. A child who is the expert in the room does not freeze.

Never correct them in front of anybody, and that includes a rehearsal with one parent watching. If something needs saying, it gets said later, alone, in one sentence, as a suggestion they can turn down.

Ask them two questions and treat the answers as final. Do they want everybody watching for all of it, or only for part of it? Do they want to be recorded? They are theirs to answer and yours to defend on the day if somebody starts negotiating with them about it.

Then agree the escape route, out loud, so it exists before it is needed. If they freeze or want to stop, what is the signal, what do you say, and where do they go? Say clearly that stopping is allowed and nothing bad happens, and then say it again on the day before they start. A young child who knows they can leave is much less likely to want to.
checklist: We rehearsed twice, both times short, and I stopped while it was still fun
I rehearsed the shape with them, where they stand and what they hold, and not the words
The pattern station is theirs and they know that whatever rule they invent is the right one
I asked them about people watching and about being recorded, and I am going to defend their answers
We agreed out loud what happens if they want to stop, and they know that stopping is allowed

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt:
The whole rehearsal in one take, all four acts, timer in shot or audible, including the bits that went wrong. Do not stop the recording and do not start again. Then, on the same recording, say your one fix out loud in a sentence and run just that act again.

Then keep rolling and answer this week's question in your own words: when is a thing finished? Use two real examples from this year, one thing you stopped working on too early and one you kept fiddling with for too long, and say how you could tell the difference afterwards but not at the time.
